speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speechtext:
I notice in the Ottawa Journal
of this morning an editorial under the caption "The Word of a Minister," which questions the veracity of ministers of the crown with regard to certain statements made on the floor of this House. It seems to me that this is a matter which affects not only

Privilege-Mr. Woodsworth
the ministers themselves but throws discredit on the House, and that it ought not to be passed without challenge.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
I have not seen the
editorial to which my hon. friend has made reference. I agree with him that any comment of the character he has mentioned is not fitting, but I think that he, along with the rest of us, will have to make some allowance for articles that appear in the Journal.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
I think perhaps I
might be permitted to read the editorial. It is not a long one, and as I say, it reflects, I believe, upon the honour of this House.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
stated his point, and the right hon. leader of the House, who is responsible to -a certain degree for the honour of the House, has declared that he has not read the article, so if the hon. gentleman will give him time to read the article, perhaps then the questions might come up.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext: May I not have the opportunity of reading the article, which, as I say, seems to reflect upon the honour of this House?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext: If it affects the honour of members of this House, certainly it is a question of privilege, but as the article has not been read by the right hon. leader of the House, and as the hon. member concluded his remarks by simply asking the right hon. leader of the House, to make a statement on the subject, I think he should give him an opportunity to at least read the editorial. I do not know the contents of the article, but if it is a question affecting the honour of the House, the hon. gentleman will have to read it first:

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
The article reads as follows:
In the House of Commons, on Friday, May 15, Sir Henry Drayton put this question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
"Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce mean to say that the whole question of the export of Carillon power is a myth and that this government has not been requested to grant it?"
Mr. Low replied:
"I say to my honorable friend without any hesitation that we have had no application for a license to export Carillon power."
Sir Henry Drayton retorted that he couldn't take seriously the idea that nothing had been said to the government about the export of power. Mr. King, the Prime Minister, then said:
"No application whatever that I am aware of has been made to the government with respect to the
217i
export of power. I am making that statement fully conscious of its significance and meaning in every particular."
That was on Friday, May 15. Yet on Monday, May 18, the government, in compliance with an order of the House, tables a return including a tentative contract with the "Carillon Industrial Corporation of Ottawa," expressly dealing with the export of power from the proposed Carillon Falls dam. Under this contract, yet unsigned, the development company is given the right to export all power developed over 100,000 horsepower.
What is the country to make of such a thing? Here you have the Prime Minister and one of his ministers solemnly assuring the House that a certain thing, of which they were both bound to have knowledge, had not taken place; only to have the assurance followed by official documents which prove that they misled the House. What possible confidence can parliament or the country have in the ministry in the face of such an occurrence ?
Nor is this the first offence of its kind. Only last week Mr. Lesueur asked the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Stewart, whether a report had not been made by an official of his department upon the oil fields of Sarnia. Mr. Stewart replied that the official in question had made no report upon the Sarnia oil fields, nor had he been asked to make one. That seemed conclusive enough; but, to the astonishment of the House, Mr. Lesueur arose, produced the report-a very lengthy one -and read it to the House.
Such things should not take place in parliament. Exaggerated statements, misleading statements, are deplorable enough when voiced by perspiring orators on the hustings, but it is a far more serious matter when ministers use parliament for seemingly deliberate misrepresentation. The anarchist could wish for nothing more likely to sap public confidence in parliamentary institutions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
That article'
seems to me comparatively mild compared to some that I have read in the Journal.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
I would just like to interject
that the article is misleading, and so far as I am concerned it is untrue. Mr. LeSueur never read the report in question. The report was handed to Mr. LeSueur by myself. He read a letter from a gentleman in which he said that he knew a report of this character was in the department.
While I am on my feet, I would just like again to state although I made a full explanation when the matter was under discussion, that the report so far as I was concerned was considered a private report. The return that was brought down, which I must confess I did not examine, did make the statement that no report was in existence. All I wish to state is that while the incident is regrettable, and no one regrets it more than I do, I was in no way guilty of misleading the House. That was not the intention at all in any particular.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. WOODSWORTH NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL ON MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS

speechtext:
I understand there are
a number of hon. gentlemen opposite, and on this side also, who desire to leave early. I want to say to them that we should propose only to put through one item-civil government. There is an increase of eight clerkships for 1925-26 over the number provided for 1924-25. This is due to the reorganization which has been effected by the Civil Service Commission in some of the branches of the department, but especially in the records division. This particular division has been carrying on for a number of years with an ever increasing amount of correspondence to be filed and registered. A large portion of the staff has been composed of temporary clerks only, although a good many of these positions have been considered by the department for a long time as being of a permanent nature. The Civil Service Commission were asked to re-organize this division on a permanent basis, which they did. in order to promote the efficiency so much desired by the department. While there is an increase of eight in the permanent positions, the whole staff of permanent and temporary clerkships combined in the department at Ottawa has been decreased by six, and the amount required to cover the combined salaries has also been decreased by $15,405 as compared with the sum provided for the fiscal year 1924-25.

The increase in the superannuation vote-I do not know what title it comes under but I call it the Calder Act moneys-would make this year's estimate very considerably in excess of last year, would it not?

Supply-Immigration

While I would not like to
say that, I imagine that generally speaking my right hon. friend is correct-that a great number of the employees in the service have taken advantage of the Calder Act, more particularly during the last-
Year.

Those retired by the
government under the Calder Act, would, in a staff of about seventy-eight, certainly involve an annual payment of anywhere from $6,000 to $10,000, would they not?

I ha.e not the figures here. I
do recall that the Treasury board incurred the displeasure of a good many civil servants by not allowing some people to take advantage of the Calder Act because it was thought they did not come within the age limit.

I notice at the foot of the page giving the details of civil government for this department-and I have observed it in the case of the votes for other departments- the statement:
Less saving estimated to be effected through superannuation and re-organization.
While there is a direct saving, I imagine, for the department, the allowance of the man who is superannuated is still a liability, but it is paid out of another fund-out of consolidated revenue, I suppose, or some other fund. Is that correct?
It is paid out of another fund.

It is not paid by the department, but comes from another fund? So that, in connection with the point made by my right hon. leader, although some men have been superannuated they still get a superannuation allowance or salary. Consequently in reality there is no saving at all to the government or to the people as a whole? In fact there is an increase very often, and there is in most cases. Take, for example, the case of a man who is in charge, we will say of a branch at a salary of $4,000 a year. He takes his superannuation under the Calder Act. We will say he is getting $3,000-I am not quoting exact figures, but that will do as an illustration. Somebody else is appointed to take his position who perhaps, will get $4,000 or very nearly that amount; perhaps he will not get the full amount, he starts at a lower salary,' say $3,500 or $3,000. But the two amounts together-the superannuation salary and the salary of the new man-would
increase the expenditure of the government.
Is not that true?
Well. I will go this far with my hon. friend and say that the Calder , Act, in my judgment, has not tended towards economy in the public service.

All right. Then, I want
to ask, why put at the bottom of the details of civil government-perhaps it is unintentional but it is certainly misleading-such a statement when there is no saving at all? The same thing is done in the case of other departments and it /may have been the practice in the past. I do not know anything about that; but it does not seem to me to be a reasonable thing to put such a statement at the bottom of the estimates when in reality, or in all probability, there has been an increase in the expenditure, and not any saving at all.

We are dealing now with the
Department of Immigration and Colonization, and each minister explains the transactions of his department when his estimates come before the committee. It is correct that we have effected an economy in the service, but I admit again that in my judgment the Calder Act has not tended towardte economy in the public service. Many people have taken advantage of the Calder Act that I believe were quite able to carry on for a while longer. But the Calder Act was there, although it is not our child, and I suppose it was only human for people to take advantage of it.
May I ask the minister if he will tell the committee just what he means by " an estimated saving of $8,000?" Who estimated it and on what basis?

Well, it is an estimate by the accountant. I direct the attention of the committee to the fact-and I think every hon. gentleman will acknowledge it, particularly ex-ministers who have had to do with the preparing of the estimates and administering public affairs-that under our system when we are compelled to provide for the payment of employees during the year, with the possibility that some of them may drop out, and taking this into consideration as well as the changes that occur, often-times the estimate is more than is really required during the year. But we must make provision for eventualities; otherwise we could not make the necessary payments. For example, take the estimates of 1923-24. The amount voted was $274,845, but the actual amount expended was $233,013.47. The following year, 1924-25, the

amount voted to provide for the salaries as laid down by the regulations-and we must follow them-was $251,235, but the amount actually expended was $221,465.91 or about $30,000 less.

As a matter of fact the scheme the government has adopted this year of putting so much saving at the end of the details of civil government for each of the departments is so much eye-wash; the minister knows it right well. Every year since Canada has been a country there would be a certain amount saved from the estimates of any department for salaries by deaths, by resignations, by the operation of the Superannuation Act when we had it, and so on. But we always had to put the full-
_ Mr. ROBB: But my right hon. friend has just said that the Superannuation Act does not result in a saving.

No, I did not say that at all; that is what the minister said. The minister said the Calder Act had not resulted in a saving, and I will come to that in a minute. There has always been an amount that would necessarily be saved in the estimate of any department, but we had to put in the amount of each salary in order that the salary might be paid if necessary.
That is right.

Now, in order to make
the estimate appear less the government has adopted an ingenious device by reducing at the beginning by a certain aggregate which they know will be saved-which always has been saved in every year in the past, indeed it may be a great deal more-making the total estimates that much less, and making it appear like a saving, whereas it is not a particle more saving than has always been the case. It is only a device to improve appearances, something at which this government has managed to develop a wonderful expertness. It is eye-wash and nothing else.

My right hon. friend will
admit it is ingenious.

I will admit they are
ingenious in misleading the public. If that is a credit, I am ready to give them credit for it, with a full heart.
That is, they are ingenious.

Yes. The minister
knows the number of retirements under the Calder Act, and knows that if he takes what is to be paid these men this year the sub' stantial cost to the country is more than last 
year. He cannot help it. On his estimates he cannot help but admit that it is considerably more. And this in the face of the reduced immigration of last year-he only received 111,000, against 148,000 the year before, and as against 148,000 of the last year of office of the late government. But what I want to commiserate with the minister on is the condition of imprisonment he suffers because of the Calder Act. "There is the act," he says, "it is not our child; we are the unfortunate heirs, and because of that act larger expense is heaped upon the government." I would like to give the minister credit, and consequently I will say that he does not believe that at all. He does not need to retire one man under the Calder Act unless he wants to-not one man. He can ignore that act-rthrow it in the waste paper basket. If the Calder Act is an expense to this country it is the fault of the government. They have not the courage to stand up and say no to civil servants who want to retire.
But we have said no.

He has sometimes said

itself. It was only in existence for a certain period.

it lived, it lived because of the act of this government; they themselves extended it.

He knows it is due to himself, if such is the fact at all, because he is the Chairman of the Treasury Board. speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not rise to say anything about the Calder Act; it is out of existence now. But I think the provision of the Superannuation Act will now pretty nearly take care of the cost of superannuation-the contributions of the civil servants to that superannuation will take care of it. It is true a very large number of people who are advanced in age took advantage of the Calder Act and asked for retirement before the expiring of the act. That was bound to happen. But, if my right hon. friend will examine the records, he will find that many of these cases were examined by a doctor suggested by the Treasury Board, and were
certified to be ill or physically incapacitated to carry on the work. What I object to is the exception taken by my hon. friend to the reduction. When the estimates have been before the House this year no one has criticized the expenditures more vigorously than my hon. friend sitting opposite, and he has asked repeatedly for the expenditures of previous years; and then if the estimate appears to be larger than the actual expenditure the criticism offered was that we were asking for more than we expended. In order to meet that, to show clearly what the estimated expenditure in my department would be, this system was adopted this year at my request, and I want to take responsibility for it. I asked them to do it in my department. Why should we ask for more money than we know we are going to expend? Why, and inflate the estimates? If there is anything misleading about it, the misleading part of it has been done in years gone by. It was in order to reduce the expenditure-my hon. friend is quite correct-and still have sufficient funds to carry on in the department. That is the reason it appears this year. It was discussed when the estimates of the Department of the Interior were up, and I again reiterate the statement made upon that occasion.
The minister has successfully turned the subject to the phase in respect of which the government is the least guilty. That I admit.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will admit there is nothing wirong about it.

speechtext: But the right hon. member claims it was misleading. I cannot understand how it would be.

By comparison with other years. You can see very plainly it may be

just as good a system, but when we take the estimates of this year and look at the total, and say that the government proposes to spend this year so much less than last year, it is not true. It merely means that you have adopted a different system, not that there is to be less expenditure. Thus, in the comparison, it is misleading to the public. I do not say that if we had started this system from the very beginning that it would not be just as good, but as to this $8,000,000 taken off here, and the $25,000,000 taken off another place, that $8,000,000 and $25,000,000 would have been off last year or the year before, or the year,before that, if this system had been adopted, for the reason that always less is expended than the amount estimated for salaries and retirements and the like. There always will be. All that is done is to lump this estimate together, and so make it appear that the government are economizing. That is all that I pointed out and that is absolutely true. The minister says that when they asked for more than they spent last year, they were severely criticized. If they were, from the mere fact that the amount asked for was more than was spent the previous year, that is an unjust criticism. I never heard it, and the minister certainly never heard me make that criticism. I have been in departments long enough to know that you have to estimate for more than you expect to spend. You cannot estimate for the exact amount. It might be that there is criticism because the margin is too large. The minister has to allow a certain margin even in estimates of salaries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have not the estimates before me and I am not sure that I have in mind the particular item to which my hon. friend is referring, I thought however that he was discussing a practice. I know that in going over the estimates it was a surprise to all of us to find that it was necessary to ask for more money than would actually be required, but this was due to an arrangement with the Civil Service Commission whereby no man can be put into a different class unless the full amount is voted for that class in advance of the time at which he becomes entitled to enter it. Assume that an official will be made a first-class clerk on January 1: we shall have to appropriate the amount that is required for that clerk just as though he were going in at the beginning of the new fiscal year, although we may not use the whole appropriation. The clerk cannot be promoted to the higher class unless parliament has given the full appropriation in the first instance. 
The result therefore is that the estimates really call for more in the way of an assumed expenditure than will be actually required as promotions are made.

I quite agree with the Prime
Minister; but I should like to point out that there is nothing new in that. If you take the estimates of 1921, 1922, 1923 and 1924, you will find appropriations that are not required in full. But you will no't find in those estimates the method which we see now put into effect. I do not know whether the Prime Minister heard the list I read before, and Which I do not suggest is complete, but I would draw his attention to one large item which I think is worthy of our consideration -the item we are discussing just now is only $8,000, it is true; 'but it is the change of method that I am dealing with, and I want to find out when that change took place. At page 64 of the estimates the Prime Minister will see an item of $250,000 for the Post Office Department and another item for the same department, at page 95, of $35,000, making a total of $285,000 treated in this particular way. So far as I know, the method now adopted in relation to these items was not pursued' prior to .the estimates of 1925, and I presume that there was a time when the government must have considered the advisability of adopting this new system. What I want to find out is when and why that change was thought necessary. The Prime Minister has given me a partial explanation, but my answer to him is that this explanation would have been just as effective in 1924 or 1923 as it is this year. I do not regard it as adequate.

I realize that this matter concerns the Department of the Secretary of State, but it is of vital importance to our immigration policy that those Canadians who have lost their Canadian status, their British citizenship, by becoming naturalized United States citizens, should be given, every opportunity to regain their Canadian status on their return to Canada with the intention of once more becoming permanent residents of this country.
